name: Overjustification Effect
description: When people already enjoy an activity, adding a salient external reward can reduce their intrinsic motivation to keep doing it once the reward disappears. Extrinsic incentives can crowd out the internal reason for acting.
design_relevance_note: Matters when points, badges, streaks, or cash-like rewards are layered onto learning, community, health, or productivity products that depend on durable self-driven engagement.
myth_risk_note: Genuine backing exists but with context-dependency and measurement sensitivity; effect appears real but more nuanced than popular accounts suggest.
prevalence_note: Common in specialist gamification, motivation, and learning-design conversations, but much less central in general-purpose UX curricula than anchoring, defaults, or confirmation bias.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of 128 studies confirmed that engagement-, completion-, and performance-contingent extrinsic rewards significantly undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation. Crucially, not all feedback is harmful: positive feedback alone actually enhanced both free-choice engagement and self-reported interest — a real, substantial nuance for any design pattern layering extrinsic rewards (badges, points, streaks) on top of an activity people might otherwise do for its own sake. Tangible rewards were also more detrimental for children than for adults.
findings.effect_size: d = -0.40 (engagement-contingent) / -0.36 (completion-contingent) / -0.28 (performance-contingent) rewards undermining free-choice intrinsic motivation; positive feedback alone: d = +0.33 (free-choice), +0.31 (self-reported interest)
findings.source_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of Experiments Examining the Effects of Extrinsic Rewards on Intrinsic Motivation

findings.description: Children with baseline intrinsic interest in an activity who then expected an extrinsic reward for doing it showed significantly less subsequent intrinsic interest than children who received an unexpected reward or no reward at all — the founding demonstration of the overjustification effect: adding an explicit extrinsic incentive for something people already enjoy doing can undermine internal motivation to keep doing it once the incentive is removed.
findings.source_title: Undermining Children's Intrinsic Interest with Extrinsic Reward: A Test of the "Overjustification" Hypothesis
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: Lepper, Greene & Nisbett's preschool drawing study: expected rewards kill intrinsic interest
applications.description: In a 1973 study, psychologists Mark Lepper, Daniel Greene, and Richard Nisbett identified preschoolers with a natural interest in drawing, then divided them into three groups: one was promised a certificate for drawing (expected reward), one received the same certificate unexpectedly after drawing (unexpected reward), and one received nothing. Two weeks later, only the expected-reward group showed a significant decline in both time spent drawing and interest in the activity -- the other two groups were unchanged. Turning a spontaneous interest into something done for an anticipated reward measurably reduced the children's intrinsic motivation to do it.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a foundational, real, peer-reviewed developmental-psychology finding about how extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no manipulator or manipulated party in the everyday sense, only a disclosed experiment on children conducted with informed teacher consent, illustrating a mechanism directly relevant to reward-based product features (badges, points, streaks) covered elsewhere in this corpus.
